1-1.text: Part one. Magnets and poles. ... This is a bar magnet. Its two ends are called poles: a north pole and a south pole.

1-2.text: The magnetic force is strongest at the poles. See how the paper clips cling to the ends, not the middle.

1-3.text: Magnets attract magnetic materials. The magnetic metals are iron, nickel and cobalt. Most steel is magnetic too, because it is mostly iron.

1-4.text: Most other metals are not magnetic: copper, aluminium and gold stay put. So do wood and plastic.

2-1.text: Part two. Attract and repel. ... Bring two magnets close. A north pole and a south pole pull together: opposite poles attract.

2-2.text: Two north poles push each other apart. So do two south poles: like poles repel.

2-3.text: Magnetism is a non-contact force. The magnet pulls the paper clip up across the gap, without touching it.

2-4.text: Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets. Each half has its own north pole and south pole.

3-1.text: Part three. Magnetic fields. ... Around every magnet is a magnetic field. It is the space where the magnet pushes or pulls on magnetic things.

3-2.text: Sprinkle iron filings round a magnet and they line up in a pattern of curved lines.

3-3.text: We draw the pattern as field lines. Outside the magnet, the arrows always go from the north pole to the south pole.

3-4.text: The lines are closest together at the poles. That is where the field is strongest.

3-5.text: A small plotting compass points along the field lines, so you can use one to map a magnet's field.

4-1.text: Part four. Compasses and the Earth. ... A compass needle is a tiny magnet that can spin freely. Wherever you stand, it settles pointing north.

4-2.text: That's because the Earth has a magnetic field, a bit like a giant bar magnet inside it.

4-3.text: The compass needle lines up with the Earth's field, so its north end points towards the North Pole.

4-4.text: Here's a twist! Opposite poles attract, so the Earth's magnet must have its south pole up near the Arctic. That's what pulls the north end of the needle.

5-1.text: Part five. Electromagnets. ... An electric current flowing in a wire makes a magnetic field around the wire. Look how the compasses turn.

5-2.text: Wind the wire into a coil and the field is stronger. It has the same shape as a bar magnet's field.

5-3.text: Put an iron core inside the coil and the field gets much stronger. Now it is an electromagnet.

5-4.text: Switch the current off and the magnetism stops. The paper clips drop!

5-5.text: To make an electromagnet stronger, use more turns of wire, a bigger current, or an iron core.

6-1.text: Part six. Using electromagnets. ... The best thing about an electromagnet is that you can switch it on and off.

6-2.text: A scrapyard crane uses a huge electromagnet to lift old cars. Switch it off and the car drops.

6-3.text: In an electric bell, the electromagnet pulls an iron arm and the hammer hits the bell. This breaks the circuit, the arm springs back, and it all starts again.

6-4.text: Electromagnets are also in loudspeakers, electric door locks and the scanners used in hospitals.
